name: Ollama
summary: A local model-serving product that combines a CLI, HTTP API, model manifests and import tooling, and backend-specific runner processes behind a host daemon.

features.name: Daemon and API service boundary
features.description: Ollama exposes a host service with REST operations for running and managing models. The fixed source separates API types/client code from server routing and request handling, while official documentation presents the API as a local endpoint.
benefits: Allows multiple local clients and integrations to share one model service
Separates request protocol handling from model execution internals
costs: A daemon becomes a shared lifecycle, logging, and resource-management boundary
Local API compatibility must be maintained for CLI and external clients

features.name: Model manifest and import lifecycle
features.description: The repository contains model, manifest, create, and transfer packages, and the official Modelfile/import documentation defines model construction and import operations. This makes model identity and assembly a managed lifecycle above backend execution.
benefits: Gives local models stable names and repeatable construction inputs
Separates model packaging and transfer from request execution
costs: Manifest, blob, and imported-weight compatibility create storage and migration obligations
Model metadata can select behavior that differs across backend capabilities

features.name: Backend-specific runner dispatch
features.description: The fixed source separates LLM orchestration from llama.cpp and MLX-related backend directories, and the official project overview identifies supported backends. The product therefore dispatches model work through backend-specific runtime boundaries rather than one universal execution implementation.
benefits: Adapts local inference to different operating-system and accelerator capabilities
Keeps backend-specific code behind a higher-level model-serving interface
costs: Backend differences can change memory use, supported features, and output behavior
Runner startup and process/resource coordination add latency and failure states

features.name: CLI and API client boundary
features.description: Ollama provides a command-line surface for model operations and integrations while also publishing an HTTP API and Go client package. These are control clients over the service/model lifecycle, not separate inference runtimes.
benefits: Supports interactive local use and programmatic automation over the same service
Allows integrations to avoid coupling directly to backend runners
costs: CLI, API, and client representations must remain semantically aligned
Control-plane errors can be confused with model or runner failures without explicit state reporting

mathematical_views.question: How does a model move from manifest/import inputs through creation, storage, availability, serving, and removal?
assumptions: Manifest and blob state identify a model artifact
Import/create operations may fail before serving is possible
The model abstracts exact file formats, storage paths, and download scheduling

mathematical_views.question: Which model runner and host resource boundary can satisfy an API request for a given model?
assumptions: A request identifies a model and operation
Model metadata and host capabilities constrain runner selection
The view abstracts token scheduling and accelerator kernels

mathematical_views.question: How do CLI commands, API clients, daemon routes, and backend runners compose into one local serving product?
assumptions: CLI and API clients are control-plane vertices
The daemon mediates model and runner lifecycle
Structural composition does not imply that all clients expose identical semantics

benefits: One local service can serve CLI, library, and application clients
costs: Daemon lifecycle and API compatibility become shared operational concerns

benefits: Model packaging and naming are explicit and reusable
costs: Artifact, manifest, and backend compatibility increase storage complexity

benefits: The service can select platform-appropriate inference implementations
costs: Runner variation complicates performance and feature portability

benefits: Interactive and automated control paths share one service contract
costs: Multiple control surfaces require consistent lifecycle and error semantics
